sections.title: Section I
sections.instructions: Attempt Questions 1 to 10. Allow about 15 minutes for this section.

stem.t: What is the remainder when $x^{100}$ is divided by $(x - 1)^2$?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: Write $x^{100} = (x - 1)^2Q(x) + ax + b$. Putting $x = 1$ gives $a + b = 1$. Differentiating, $100x^{99} = 2(x - 1)Q(x) + (x - 1)^2Q'(x) + a$, and $x = 1$ gives $a = 100$. So $b = -99$ and the remainder is $100x - 99$.

classification.content: Remainders; multiple zeros; differentiation

stem.t: The diagram shows a regular polygon with 12 sides and one of the triangles that can be formed by joining three of its vertices.
How many of the triangles that can be formed in this way are acute-angled?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: The vertices lie on a circle, and an angle of the triangle is acute exactly when the arc opposite it is less than a semicircle. Going around the circle, the three arcs between the chosen vertices contain $p$, $q$ and $r$ sides, where $p + q + r = 12$, and the triangle is acute-angled exactly when $p, q, r \le 5$. The ordered possibilities are $(2, 5, 5)$ in 3 orders, $(3, 4, 5)$ in 6 orders and $(4, 4, 4)$: 10 in all. Choosing the starting vertex in 12 ways counts each triangle 3 times, so the number is $\dfrac{12 \times 10}{3} = 40$.

classification.content: Counting techniques; circle geometry

stem.t: Which of the following is the graph of $y = \sin^{-1}(\cos x) + \cos^{-1}(\sin x)$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: Since $\sin^{-1}u + \cos^{-1}u = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\ y = \pi - \left[\cos^{-1}(\cos x) + \sin^{-1}(\sin x)\right]$. For $0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2}$ both terms in the bracket equal $x$, so $y = \pi - 2x$. For $\frac{\pi}{2} \le x \le \pi$ they are $x$ and $\pi - x$, so $y = 0$. For $\pi \le x \le \frac{3\pi}{2}$ they are $2\pi - x$ and $\pi - x$, so $y = 2x - 2\pi$. For $\frac{3\pi}{2} \le x \le 2\pi$ they are $2\pi - x$ and $x - 2\pi$, so $y = \pi$. The graph falls from $\pi$ to 0, stays at 0, rises to $\pi$ and stays at $\pi$.

classification.content: Graphs of inverse trigonometric functions; complementary angles

stem.t: The triangle $ABC$ is equilateral with sides of length 3, and $P$ is a point on the circle that passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$.
What is the value of $PA^2 + PB^2 + PC^2$?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: Take the centre $O$ as origin, with position vectors $\underset{\sim}{a}, \underset{\sim}{b}, \underset{\sim}{c}, \underset{\sim}{p}$, each of length $R$. By symmetry $\underset{\sim}{a} + \underset{\sim}{b} + \underset{\sim}{c} = \underset{\sim}{0}$. Then $PA^2 + PB^2 + PC^2 = 3\left|\underset{\sim}{p}\right|^2 + \left|\underset{\sim}{a}\right|^2 + \left|\underset{\sim}{b}\right|^2 + \left|\underset{\sim}{c}\right|^2 - 2\,\underset{\sim}{p}\cdot\left(\underset{\sim}{a} + \underset{\sim}{b} + \underset{\sim}{c}\right) = 6R^2$. The circle has radius $R = \dfrac{3}{2\sin 60^\circ} = \sqrt3$, so the value is 18 for every position of $P$.

classification.content: Vectors in two dimensions; scalar product

stem.t: The random variable $X$ has a binomial distribution with $n = 20$ and probability of success $p$. It is given that $P(X = 7) = P(X = 8)$.

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: $\dfrac{P(X = 8)}{P(X = 7)} = \dfrac{\binom{20}{8}}{\binom{20}{7}} \times \dfrac{p}{1 - p} = \dfrac{13}{8} \times \dfrac{p}{1 - p}$. Setting this equal to 1 gives $13p = 8 - 8p$, so $p = \dfrac{8}{21}$.

classification.content: Binomial distribution; binomial coefficients

stem.t: The diagram shows the slope field of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x - y$.
Which of the following is true of the solution curve that passes through the point $(0, -2)$?

blocks.t: It has a minimum turning point on the line $y = x$.
It has a maximum turning point on the line $y = x$.
It has no stationary points and it is concave up for all $x$.
It has no stationary points and it is concave down for all $x$.

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: The line $y = x - 1$ is a solution curve, since its gradient is 1 and $x - (x - 1) = 1$. Solution curves cannot cross, so the curve through $(0, -2)$ stays below this line, where $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x - y > 1$. So there are no stationary points. Also $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 1 - \dfrac{dy}{dx} < 0$, so the curve is concave down for all $x$. (A stationary point would have to lie on $y = x$, which is above the line $y = x - 1$.)

classification.content: Slope fields; solution curves; concavity

stem.t: How many real solutions does the equation $\sin^{-1}(\sin x) = \dfrac{x}{5}$ have?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: The graph of $y = \sin^{-1}(\sin x)$ is a zigzag of line segments of gradient $\pm1$ through $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{5\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, …, and it is odd. For $x > 0$ the line $y = \frac{x}{5}$ meets the segment $y = \pi - x$ at $x = \frac{5\pi}{6}$ and passes exactly through the peak $\left(\frac{5\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$; beyond that the line is above $\frac{\pi}{2}$. With $x = 0$ and the two negative solutions, there are 5 solutions.

classification.content: Inverse trigonometric functions; graphical solution of equations

stem.t: What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} x^2\cos^{-1}x\,dx$?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: Let $I$ be the integral. The substitution $x = -u$ and the identity $\cos^{-1}(-u) = \pi - \cos^{-1}u$ give $I = \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}u^2\left(\pi - \cos^{-1}u\right)du = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} - I$. Hence $I = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

classification.content: Integration by substitution; symmetry of inverse trigonometric functions

stem.t: The diagram shows the curve $x = \sin t$, $y = \sin 2t$, where $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.
What is the area of the shaded loop?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: For $0 \le t \le \frac{\pi}{2}$, $y = 2\sin t\cos t = 2x\sqrt{1 - x^2}$, and the lower half of the loop is its reflection in the $x$-axis. The area is $2\displaystyle\int_0^1 2x\sqrt{1 - x^2}\,dx = 2\left[-\tfrac23\left(1 - x^2\right)^{\frac32}\right]_0^1 = \dfrac43$.

classification.content: Parametric form; areas; integration by substitution

stem.t: Some of the integers from 1 to 20 are chosen.
What is the smallest number of integers that must be chosen to be certain that two of the chosen integers differ by exactly 4?

text.t: Correct option.

sampleAnswer.t: Split the integers into the four chains $1, 5, 9, 13, 17$; $\ 2, 6, 10, 14, 18$; $\ 3, 7, 11, 15, 19$; $\ 4, 8, 12, 16, 20$. Two integers differ by 4 exactly when they are neighbours in a chain. At most 3 integers can be chosen from a chain of 5 with no two neighbours, so 12 integers can be chosen with no two differing by 4 (for example $1, 9, 17, 2, 10, 18, \ldots$). If 13 are chosen, some chain contains at least 4 of them, and two of those are neighbours. So the answer is 13.

classification.content: The pigeonhole principle

sections.title: Section II
sections.instructions: Attempt Questions 11 to 14. Allow about 1 hour and 45 minutes for this section. Show relevant mathematical reasoning and/or calculations.

prompt.t: Let $P(x) = x^3 - 18x^2 + 104x - k$, where $k$ is a real number.
Whenever $P(x)$ has three distinct real zeros $a$, $b$ and $c$, these zeros are the side lengths of a triangle, and the area of the triangle is
\sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}, \qquad\text{where } s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}.
**(Do NOT prove these two facts.)**
Find all values of $k$ for which $P(x)$ has three distinct real zeros.

text.t: Provides the correct set of values with justification
Finds the stationary values of $P(x)$, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: $P'(x) = 3x^2 - 36x + 104 = 0$ when $x = 6 \pm \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$. Since the leading coefficient is positive, $P$ has a local maximum at $x = 6 - \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ and a local minimum at $x = 6 + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$, and $P$ has three distinct real zeros if and only if the local maximum value is positive and the local minimum value is negative.

Now $x^3 - 18x^2 + 104x - 192 = (x - 4)(x - 6)(x - 8)$, and with $x = 6 + u$ this is $u(u - 2)(u + 2) = u^3 - 4u$. So $P(6 + u) = u^3 - 4u + 192 - k$. When $u = \mp\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$, $\ u^3 - 4u = \pm\left(\dfrac{8}{\sqrt3} - \dfrac{8}{3\sqrt3}\right) = \pm\dfrac{16}{3\sqrt3} = \pm\dfrac{16\sqrt3}{9}$.
The conditions are $\dfrac{16\sqrt3}{9} + 192 - k > 0$ and $-\dfrac{16\sqrt3}{9} + 192 - k < 0$, that is, $\left|k - 192\right| < \dfrac{16\sqrt3}{9}$.

classification.content: Zeros and coefficients of polynomials; stationary points; cosine rule

parts.label: (ii)

prompt.t: Find the area of the triangle in terms of $k$.

text.t: Provides the correct area
Finds $s = 9$, or recognises that $(s - a)(s - b)(s - c) = P(s)$

sampleAnswer.t: The sum of the zeros is $a + b + c = 18$, so $s = 9$. Since $P(x) = (x - a)(x - b)(x - c)$,
Hence the area is $\sqrt{9(207 - k)} = 3\sqrt{207 - k}$.

classification.content: Zeros and coefficients of polynomials; stationary points; cosine rule

parts.keyChecks: verified by tools/papers/verify/p01.py: Heron's formula on numeric roots of x^3-18x^2+104x-k for 30 random k in range; max err 7e-15

parts.label: (iii)

prompt.t: Find the exact value of $k$ for which the triangle is right-angled.

text.t: Provides the correct value with justification
Shows that the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{58}$, or equivalent merit
Finds $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 116$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: If the triangle is right-angled with hypotenuse $c$ then $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, so $2c^2 = 116$ and $c = \sqrt{58}$. Hence $P\left(\sqrt{58}\right) = 0$:
58\sqrt{58} - 18 \times 58 + 104\sqrt{58} - k = 0, \qquad\text{so}\qquad k = 162\sqrt{58} - 1044.

This value is approximately $189.76$, which satisfies the condition in part (i) ($192 - \frac{16\sqrt3}{9} \approx 188.92$). Then $\sqrt{58}$ is a side, and the other two sides satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = 116 - 58 = c^2$, so the triangle is right-angled. Hence $k = 162\sqrt{58} - 1044$.

classification.content: Zeros and coefficients of polynomials; stationary points; cosine rule

parts.keyChecks: verified by tools/papers/verify/p01.py: scan of the whole admissible k range for a^2+b^2=c^2 via numeric roots + bisection: exactly one solution 189.75524315

prompt.t: Prove by mathematical induction that, for all integers $n \ge 1$,
(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3) \times \cdots \times (2n) = 2^n \times 1 \times 3 \times 5 \times \cdots \times (2n - 1).

text.t: Provides a correct proof
Verifies the base case and makes substantial progress with the inductive step
Verifies the base case, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: When $n = 1$, the left-hand side is $2$ and the right-hand side is $2^1 \times 1 = 2$, so the statement is true for $n = 1$.
Assume that the statement is true for $n = k$, that is, $(k + 1)(k + 2) \times \cdots \times (2k) = 2^k \times 1 \times 3 \times \cdots \times (2k - 1)$.
For $n = k + 1$ the left-hand side is
which is the statement for $n = k + 1$. Hence, by mathematical induction, the statement is true for all integers $n \ge 1$.

classification.content: Proof by mathematical induction; counting techniques; probability

prompt.t: In the first round of a tournament, $2n$ players are split into $n$ pairs, and the two players in each pair play each other. Show that the number of ways in which the players can be split into pairs is $1 \times 3 \times 5 \times \cdots \times (2n - 1)$.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration
Obtains $\dfrac{(2n)!}{2^n\,n!}$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: Arrange the $2n$ players in a line, in $(2n)!$ ways, and pair the 1st with the 2nd, the 3rd with the 4th, and so on. Each way of splitting the players into pairs arises from $2^n \times n!$ of these arrangements (the two players in each pair in either order, and the $n$ pairs in any order). So the number of ways is
\frac{(2n)!}{2^n\,n!} = \frac{(n + 1)(n + 2) \times \cdots \times (2n)}{2^n} = 1 \times 3 \times 5 \times \cdots \times (2n - 1), \quad\text{by part (i)}.

classification.content: Proof by mathematical induction; counting techniques; probability

parts.label: (iii)

prompt.t: The $2n$ players have different rankings, and in every game the player with the higher ranking wins. The pairs are chosen at random. Let $p_n$ be the probability that the $n$ winners in the first round are the $n$ highest-ranked players. Find $p_n$, and show that $p_n \le \left(\dfrac23\right)^{n-1}$.

text.t: Provides the correct probability and a correct proof of the inequality
Finds $p_n$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: The $n$ highest-ranked players all win exactly when each of them is paired with one of the $n$ lowest-ranked players (if two of them were paired, one would lose). The highest-ranked $n$ can be matched with the lowest-ranked $n$ in $n!$ ways, so by part (ii)
p_n = \frac{n!}{1 \times 3 \times 5 \times \cdots \times (2n - 1)} = \frac11 \times \frac23 \times \frac35 \times \cdots \times \frac{n}{2n - 1}.

For $k \ge 2$, $\ \dfrac{k}{2k - 1} \le \dfrac23$, because $3k \le 4k - 2$. The first factor is 1 and each of the other $n - 1$ factors is at most $\dfrac23$, so $p_n \le \left(\dfrac23\right)^{n-1}$.

classification.content: Proof by mathematical induction; counting techniques; probability

parts.keyChecks: verified by tools/papers/verify/p01.py: exhaustive enumeration of all pairings n=1..5 (winners = top n gives 1,2/3,2/5,8/35,8/63); inequality checked n<=79

prompt.t: A prize of $1 is offered for solving a puzzle. Each of $n + 1$ contestants, one of whom is Alice, solves the puzzle with probability $p$, independently of the others, where $0 < p < 1$ and $n \ge 1$ is an integer. The prize is shared equally among the contestants who solve the puzzle. Let $q = 1 - p$.
Let $E$ dollars be the expected value of the amount that Alice wins. Show that $E = \dfrac{1 - q^{\,n+1}}{n + 1}$.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration
Writes the expected value as a sum and uses $\binom{n}{k}\frac{1}{k + 1} = \frac{1}{n + 1}\binom{n + 1}{k + 1}$, or equivalent merit
Writes a correct expression for the expected value as a sum, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: Alice wins $\dfrac{1}{k + 1}$ dollars if she solves the puzzle and exactly $k$ of the other $n$ contestants solve it. The number of the others who solve it has a binomial distribution, so the expected value is
E = p\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}p^kq^{\,n-k} \times \frac{1}{k + 1}.
Now $\dbinom{n}{k}\dfrac{1}{k + 1} = \dfrac{n!}{(k + 1)!\,(n - k)!} = \dfrac{1}{n + 1}\dbinom{n + 1}{k + 1}$, so
since the sum contains every term of the expansion of $(p + q)^{n+1}$ except $q^{\,n+1}$.

classification.content: Binomial distribution; expected value; binomial coefficients; inequalities using calculus

prompt.t: Explain how the result of part (i) can be obtained without evaluating a sum.

text.t: Provides a correct explanation

sampleAnswer.t: The whole prize is paid out unless nobody solves the puzzle, which has probability $q^{\,n+1}$. So the expected total amount paid out is $1 - q^{\,n+1}$ dollars. The $n + 1$ contestants are in identical situations, so each has the same expected winnings, and these add up to the expected total. Hence each expects $\dfrac{1 - q^{\,n+1}}{n + 1}$ dollars.

classification.content: Binomial distribution; expected value; binomial coefficients; inequalities using calculus

prompt.t: The expected number of the other contestants who solve the puzzle is $np$.
Let $S$ dollars be the expected value of the amount that Alice wins, given that she solves the puzzle. Show that $S > \dfrac{1}{1 + np}$.

text.t: Provides a correct proof
Reduces the inequality to $1 - (n + 1)q^n + nq^{\,n+1} > 0$, or equivalent merit
Finds the expected value given that Alice solves the puzzle, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: $S = \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}p^kq^{\,n-k}\frac{1}{k + 1} = \frac{E}{p} = \frac{1 - q^{\,n+1}}{(n + 1)p}$, from part (i).
We need $\left(1 - q^{\,n+1}\right)(1 + np) > (n + 1)p$. With $p = 1 - q$,
Let $A(x) = 1 - (n + 1)x^n + nx^{n+1}$. Then $A(1) = 0$ and $A'(x) = -n(n + 1)x^{n-1}(1 - x) < 0$ for $0 < x < 1$. So $A$ is decreasing on $0 \le x \le 1$, and $A(q) > A(1) = 0$ for $0 < q < 1$.
Hence $\left(1 - q^{\,n+1}\right)(1 + np) > (n + 1)p$, that is, $S > \dfrac{1}{1 + np}$.

classification.content: Binomial distribution; expected value; binomial coefficients; inequalities using calculus

prompt.t: Two pulleys have radii $R$ and $r$, where $R \ge r$, and their centres are a distance $d$ apart, where $d > R + r$. A tight belt passes around the pulleys. The first diagram shows an open belt and the second diagram shows a crossed belt.

parts.label: (i)

prompt.t: Find the length of the open belt in terms of $R$, $r$ and $d$.

text.t: Provides the correct length with justification
Finds the length of a straight section and the angle of contact on one pulley, or equivalent merit
Finds the length of a straight section, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: Let the centres be $A$ (radius $R$) and $B$ (radius $r$), and let a straight section touch the pulleys at $T$ and $U$. The radii $AT$ and $BU$ are perpendicular to $TU$, so they are parallel. Let $N$ be the point on $AT$ with $BN \parallel UT$. Then $BNTU$ is a rectangle, $AN = R - r$ and
TU = BN = \sqrt{d^2 - (R - r)^2}.

Let $\alpha = \angle ABN$, so $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{R - r}{d}$. The radius $AT$ makes an angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha$ with $AB$, and the same is true of $BU$. So the belt is in contact with the larger pulley over an angle $2\pi - 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \pi + 2\alpha$ at its centre, and with the smaller pulley over an angle $2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \pi - 2\alpha$. The length of the belt is
2\sqrt{d^2 - (R - r)^2} + R(\pi + 2\alpha) + r(\pi - 2\alpha) = 2\sqrt{d^2 - (R - r)^2} + \pi(R + r) + 2(R - r)\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R - r}{d}\right).

classification.content: Inverse trigonometric functions; circle geometry; differentiation

parts.keyChecks: verified by tools/papers/verify/p01.py: convex-hull perimeter of two sampled discs (40000-gon) and explicit tangent geometry at 6 random (R,r,d); max err 1.7e-8

prompt.t: Show that the length of the crossed belt depends on $R$ and $r$ only through the value of $R + r$.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration
Finds the length of a straight section of the crossed belt, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: Let a straight section touch the larger pulley at $T$ and the smaller pulley at $U$. Again $AT \parallel BU$, but now $A$ and $B$ are on opposite sides of $TU$. Produce $AT$ to $N$ so that $TN = r$. Then $BNTU$ is a rectangle, $AN = R + r$ and $TU = BN = \sqrt{d^2 - (R + r)^2}$.

Let $\gamma = \angle ABN$, so $\sin\gamma = \dfrac{R + r}{d}$. Each of the radii $AT$ and $BU$ makes an angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \gamma$ with the line $AB$, and the belt is in contact with each pulley over an angle $2\pi - 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \gamma\right) = \pi + 2\gamma$. The length is
2\sqrt{d^2 - (R + r)^2} + (R + r)\left[\pi + 2\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R + r}{d}\right)\right],
which depends on $R$ and $r$ only through $R + r$.

classification.content: Inverse trigonometric functions; circle geometry; differentiation

parts.label: (iii)

prompt.t: The pulleys of a machine can be changed so that $R = c + u$ and $r = c - u$, where $c$ and $d$ are fixed and $0 \le u < c$. By part (ii), one crossed belt fits every such pair of pulleys.
Show that the length of the open belt increases as $u$ increases, and find the exact amount by which the open belt for $u = 1$ is longer than the open belt for $u = 0$ when $d = 4$.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration and the correct exact value
Shows that $\dfrac{dL}{du} = 4\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{2u}{d}\right)$, or equivalent merit
Writes $L$ in terms of $u$ and attempts to differentiate, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: Let $L$ be the length of the open belt. With $R + r = 2c$ and $R - r = 2u$, part (i) gives $L = 2\sqrt{d^2 - 4u^2} + 2\pi c + 4u\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{2u}{d}\right)$. Then
\frac{dL}{du} = \frac{-8u}{\sqrt{d^2 - 4u^2}} + 4\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2u}{d}\right) + 4u \times \frac{\frac{2}{d}}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{4u^2}{d^2}}} = 4\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2u}{d}\right),
since the last term equals $\dfrac{8u}{\sqrt{d^2 - 4u^2}}$. This is positive for $u > 0$, so $L$ increases as $u$ increases. (An open belt that fits equal pulleys is too short for every other pair.)
When $d = 4$: $\ L(1) - L(0) = \left[2\sqrt{12} + 2\pi c + 4\sin^{-1}\tfrac12\right] - \left[8 + 2\pi c\right] = 4\sqrt3 + \dfrac{2\pi}{3} - 8$.

classification.content: Inverse trigonometric functions; circle geometry; differentiation

parts.keyChecks: verified by tools/papers/verify/p01.py: convex-hull belt lengths (c=1.5,d=4,u=1 minus u=0) = 1.0225983 vs closed form 1.0225983

prompt.t: The size of a fish stock at time $t$ years is $x$ units. When the stock is fished at a constant rate of $h$ units per year, it changes according to
\frac{dx}{dt} = x(1 - x) - h.
The stock is *wiped out* when $x$ reaches 0. The diagram shows the graph of $y = x(1 - x)$ and three possible values of $h$.

parts.label: (i)

prompt.t: Suppose that $h = \dfrac14$. Find the time at which a stock with $x = \dfrac14$ when $t = 0$ is wiped out, and show that a stock with $x > \dfrac12$ when $t = 0$ is never wiped out.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration of both results
Solves the differential equation and establishes one result, or equivalent merit
Writes $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\left(x - \frac12\right)^2$ and separates the variables, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = x - x^2 - \dfrac14 = -\left(x - \dfrac12\right)^2$. For $x \ne \dfrac12$, $\displaystyle\int\frac{-dx}{\left(x - \frac12\right)^2} = \int dt$, so $\dfrac{1}{x - \frac12} = t + C$.

If $x = \dfrac14$ when $t = 0$ then $C = -4$ and $x = \dfrac12 + \dfrac{1}{t - 4}$. This decreases from $\dfrac14$ for $0 \le t < 4$, and $x = 0$ when $\dfrac{1}{t - 4} = -\dfrac12$, that is, when $t = 2$.
If $x = x_0 > \dfrac12$ when $t = 0$ then $C = \dfrac{1}{x_0 - \frac12} > 0$, and $x = \dfrac12 + \dfrac{1}{t + C} > \dfrac12$ for all $t \ge 0$. So the stock is never wiped out.

classification.content: Modelling with differential equations; inverse trigonometric functions; limits

parts.keyChecks: verified by tools/papers/verify/p01.py: RK4 of dx/dt=x(1-x)-1/4 from x(0)=1/4 hits 0 at t=2.000000; x0>1/2 never wiped out

prompt.t: Suppose that $h > \dfrac14$, and let $a = \sqrt{h - \dfrac14}$. The stock has size $x_0$ when $t = 0$. Find the time $T$ at which the stock is wiped out, and deduce that every stock, however large, is wiped out in less than $\dfrac{\pi}{a}$ years.

text.t: Provides the correct time and the deduction
Finds the correct time, or equivalent merit
Writes $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\left[\left(x - \frac12\right)^2 + a^2\right]$ and separates the variables, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\left[\left(x - \dfrac12\right)^2 + a^2\right] < 0$, so $x$ decreases and $\dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{-1}{\left(x - \frac12\right)^2 + a^2}$. Hence

T = \int_{0}^{x_0}\frac{dx}{\left(x - \frac12\right)^2 + a^2} = \frac1a\left[\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x - \frac12}{a}\right)\right]_0^{x_0} = \frac1a\left[\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2x_0 - 1}{2a}\right) + \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{2a}\right)\right].
Each inverse tangent is less than $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $T < \dfrac1a\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{a}$ for every $x_0$.

classification.content: Modelling with differential equations; inverse trigonometric functions; limits

prompt.t: Suppose that $x_0 = \dfrac14$. Show that, as $h$ decreases towards $\dfrac14$, the time $T$ in part (ii) approaches the time found in part (i).

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration
Writes $T$ in a form such as $\dfrac1a\left[\tan^{-1}4a - \tan^{-1}2a\right]$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: With $x_0 = \dfrac14$, $\ T = \dfrac1a\left[\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2a}\right) - \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{4a}\right)\right]$. For $u > 0$, $\tan^{-1}\dfrac1u = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1}u$, so
T = \frac{\tan^{-1}4a - \tan^{-1}2a}{a} = 4 \times \frac{\tan^{-1}4a}{4a} - 2 \times \frac{\tan^{-1}2a}{2a}.

As $u \to 0$, $\dfrac{\tan^{-1}u}{u} \to 1$ (put $u = \tan\theta$: $\dfrac{\theta}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac{\theta}{\sin\theta} \times \cos\theta \to 1$). As $h \to \dfrac14$ from above, $a \to 0$, so $T \to 4 - 2 = 2$, which is the time found in part (i).

prompt.t: A vessel is formed by rotating a curve in the first quadrant, which starts at the origin $O$, about the $y$-axis. Water drains from the vessel through a small hole at $O$. When the depth of the water is $h$, the radius of the water surface is $x$ and the volume of water is decreasing at the rate $k\sqrt{h}$, where $k$ is a positive constant.
Show that $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = -\dfrac{k\sqrt{h}}{\pi x^2}$.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration
Shows that $\dfrac{dV}{dh} = \pi x^2$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: When the depth is $h$, the volume of water is $V = \pi\displaystyle\int_0^h x^2\,dy$, where $x$ is the radius of the vessel at height $y$. Hence $\dfrac{dV}{dh} = \pi x^2$, with $x$ the radius at height $h$. By the chain rule,
-k\sqrt{h} = \frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{dV}{dh} \times \frac{dh}{dt} = \pi x^2\,\frac{dh}{dt}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{dh}{dt} = -\frac{k\sqrt{h}}{\pi x^2}.

prompt.t: A designer wants a vessel in which the depth of the water halves in every minute, at every depth.

Show that $x^4y$ would have to be constant along the curve that is rotated. Show also that, however small the positive number $\varepsilon$ is, the part of such a vessel between the heights $y = \varepsilon$ and $y = H$ would hold less than $\dfrac{2k\sqrt{H}}{\ln 2}$ units of water, with $t$ measured in minutes.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration of both results
Shows that $x^4y$ is constant, or equivalent merit
Obtains $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = -h\ln 2$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: If the depth halves in every minute then $h = h_0 \times 2^{-t} = h_0e^{-t\ln 2}$, so $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = -\lambda h$, where $\lambda = \ln 2$.

By part (i), $\dfrac{k\sqrt{h}}{\pi x^2} = \lambda h$ at every depth, so every point of the curve satisfies $x^2 = \dfrac{k}{\pi\lambda\sqrt{y}}$, that is, $x^4y = \dfrac{k^2}{\pi^2\lambda^2}$, a constant.
The volume between the heights $\varepsilon$ and $H$ is
\pi\int_\varepsilon^H x^2\,dy = \frac{k}{\lambda}\int_\varepsilon^H y^{-\frac12}\,dy = \frac{2k}{\lambda}\left(\sqrt{H} - \sqrt{\varepsilon}\right) < \frac{2k\sqrt{H}}{\ln 2}.
(The vessel becomes wider without limit near the bottom, but it holds only a bounded amount of water, and it never empties.)

prompt.t: A ball is projected from a point $O$ on horizontal ground with speed $V$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, and it lands at the point $A$. At time $t$ after projection the ball is at the point $P$ with position vector
Vt\cos\theta\,\underset{\sim}{i} + \left(Vt\sin\theta - \tfrac12gt^2\right)\underset{\sim}{j}
relative to $O$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. **(Do NOT prove this.)**
A camera at $O$ and a camera at $A$ both follow the ball. While the ball is in flight, $OP$ and $AP$ make angles $\phi$ and $\psi$ with the ground, as shown.
Show that $\tan\phi = \tan\theta - \dfrac{gt}{2V\cos\theta}$.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration

sampleAnswer.t: $\tan\phi = \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{Vt\sin\theta - \frac12gt^2}{Vt\cos\theta} = \tan\theta - \dfrac{gt}{2V\cos\theta}$.

classification.content: Projectile motion; trigonometric identities; rates of change; quadratic inequalities

prompt.t: Show that $\tan\phi + \tan\psi = \tan\theta$ throughout the flight.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration
Finds $OA$ or the time of flight and writes an expression for $\tan\psi$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: The ball lands when $Vt\sin\theta = \frac12gt^2$, that is, at time $T = \dfrac{2V\sin\theta}{g}$, and $OA = VT\cos\theta$. Since $V\sin\theta = \frac12gT$,
\tan\psi = \frac{y}{OA - x} = \frac{t\left(\frac12gT - \frac12gt\right)}{V\cos\theta\,(T - t)} = \frac{gt}{2V\cos\theta}.
Adding the result of part (i), $\tan\phi + \tan\psi = \tan\theta$.

prompt.t: Find, in terms of $\phi$, the rate at which the camera at $O$ is turning, and deduce that the two cameras are turning at the same rate only when the ball is at its highest point.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration and deduction
Finds the rate of turning of the camera at $O$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: Differentiating the result of part (i) with respect to $t$, $\ \sec^2\phi\,\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = -\dfrac{g}{2V\cos\theta}$, so $\phi$ decreases at the rate $\dfrac{g\cos^2\phi}{2V\cos\theta}$. Similarly, from $\tan\psi = \dfrac{gt}{2V\cos\theta}$, $\psi$ increases at the rate $\dfrac{g\cos^2\psi}{2V\cos\theta}$.

The rates are equal when $\cos^2\phi = \cos^2\psi$. As $\phi$ and $\psi$ are acute (or zero), this happens only when $\phi = \psi$, so $\tan\phi = \tan\psi = \frac12\tan\theta$ by part (ii). Then $\dfrac{gt}{2V\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{2\cos\theta}$, so $t = \dfrac{V\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{T}{2}$, which is when the ball is at its highest point.

prompt.t: Suppose that $\tan\theta > 2$. Find, in simplest form, the length of time for which $\angle OPA$ is acute.

text.t: Provides the correct length of time in simplest form
Obtains a correct quadratic inequality in $t$ or in $\tan\psi$, or equivalent merit
Shows that $\angle OPA$ is acute when $\tan\phi\tan\psi > 1$, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: $\angle OPA = \pi - \phi - \psi$, which is acute when $\phi > \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \psi$. For $0 < t < T$ both angles are acute, so this is equivalent to $\tan\phi > \cot\psi$, that is, to $\tan\phi\tan\psi > 1$.

Let $u = \tan\psi = \dfrac{gt}{2V\cos\theta}$. By part (ii) the condition is $u(\tan\theta - u) > 1$, that is, $u^2 - u\tan\theta + 1 < 0$. As $\tan\theta > 2$, this quadratic has two real zeros, which differ by $\sqrt{\tan^2\theta - 4}$, and the inequality holds between them. (Both zeros lie between 0 and $\tan\theta$, so these times are during the flight.) Since $t = \dfrac{2V\cos\theta}{g}\,u$, the length of time is
\frac{2V\cos\theta}{g}\sqrt{\tan^2\theta - 4} = \frac{2V}{g}\sqrt{\sin^2\theta - 4\cos^2\theta} = \frac{2V}{g}\sqrt{1 - 5\cos^2\theta}.

prompt.t: A committee has $2m - 1$ members, where $m \ge 2$. Each member, independently of the others, reaches the correct decision with probability $p$. The committee decides by majority vote. Let $M(p)$ be the probability that the decision of the committee is correct.

text.t: Provides a correct demonstration
Differentiates the sum and rewrites the coefficients so that terms cancel, or equivalent merit
Writes $M(p)$ as a sum of binomial probabilities, or equivalent merit

sampleAnswer.t: Let $n = 2m - 1$ and $q = 1 - p$. The decision is correct when at least $m$ members are correct, so
M(p) = \sum_{j=m}^{n}\binom{n}{j}p^jq^{\,n-j}, \qquad M'(p) = \sum_{j=m}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\left[jp^{j-1}q^{\,n-j} - (n - j)p^jq^{\,n-j-1}\right].
Now $j\dbinom{n}{j} = n\dbinom{n - 1}{j - 1}$ and $(n - j)\dbinom{n}{j} = n\dbinom{n - 1}{j}$ (the latter is 0 when $j = n$). So
M'(p) = n\sum_{j=m}^{n}\left[a_j - a_{j+1}\right], \qquad\text{where } a_j = \binom{n - 1}{j - 1}p^{j-1}q^{\,n-j} \text{ and } a_{n+1} = 0.
The sum telescopes to $a_m$, so $M'(p) = n\dbinom{n - 1}{m - 1}p^{m-1}q^{\,n-m} = (2m - 1)\dbinom{2m - 2}{m - 1}p^{m-1}(1 - p)^{m-1}$.

prompt.t: Deduce the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^{m-1}(1 - x)^{m-1}\,dx$.

text.t: Provides the correct value with justification

sampleAnswer.t: $M(0) = 0$ and $M(1) = 1$, so $\displaystyle\int_0^1 M'(p)\,dp = 1$. By part (i), $\ \displaystyle\int_0^1 x^{m-1}(1 - x)^{m-1}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{(2m - 1)\binom{2m - 2}{m - 1}}$.

prompt.t: Show that if $\dfrac12 < p < 1$ then the committee is more likely to be correct than a single member is.

text.t: Provides a correct proof
Shows that $M(p) - p$ is zero at $p = \frac12$ and $p = 1$ and that its derivative is decreasing, or equivalent merit
Shows that $M\left(\frac12\right) = \frac12$, or considers the derivative of $M(p) - p$

sampleAnswer.t: Let $g(p) = M(p) - p$. When $p = \dfrac12$, a majority for the correct decision and a majority for the wrong decision are equally likely, and one of them occurs because the number of members is odd. So $M\left(\dfrac12\right) = \dfrac12$ and $g\left(\dfrac12\right) = 0$. Also $g(1) = 0$.

By part (i), $g'(p) = c\,\bigl[p(1 - p)\bigr]^{m-1} - 1$, where $c > 0$. For $\dfrac12 \le p \le 1$ the quantity $p(1 - p)$ decreases as $p$ increases, and $m - 1 \ge 1$, so $g'(p)$ is decreasing, and $g'(1) = -1 < 0$.

If $g'\left(\dfrac12\right) \le 0$ then $g'(p) < 0$ for $\dfrac12 < p \le 1$ and $g(1) < g\left(\dfrac12\right)$, which is false. So $g'\left(\dfrac12\right) > 0$, and there is one value $p_0$ such that $g'(p) > 0$ for $\dfrac12 \le p < p_0$ and $g'(p) < 0$ for $p_0 < p \le 1$. Hence $g$ increases from 0 and then decreases to 0, so $g(p) > 0$ for $\dfrac12 < p < 1$. That is, $M(p) > p$.
